brandPrescribing.t: Prescribe insulin by brand name (SPS, citing NICE guidance), and make sure the patient gets a device they have been trained to use. Where one brand comes in more than one strength or device, the brand name alone is not enough: also state the strength and device (SPS).

src.q: NICE guidance recommends insulins are prescribed by brand name.

items.t: Dose is individual and set by the physician; usual total requirement 0.3 to 1.0 IU/kg/day (one UK SmPC). Soluble insulin: before a meal or snack, alone or with intermediate/long-acting insulin; follow each injection with a carbohydrate meal or snack within 30 minutes.

src.q: The dosage should be determined by the physician, according to the requirement of the patient.
The individual insulin requirement is usually between 0.3 and 1.0 international unit/kg/day.
It can be used alone or in combination with intermediate-acting or long-acting insulin before a meal or a snack.
An injection should be followed within 30 minutes by a meal or snack containing carbohydrates.

items.t: Isophane: once or several times daily as decided by the physician; alone, mixed with fast-acting insulin, or as basal insulin (evening and/or morning) with fast-acting insulin at meals. Usual total requirement 0.3 to 1.0 IU/kg/day.

src.q: The physician determines whether one or several daily injections are necessary. Insulatard may be used alone or mixed with fast-acting insulin.
In intensive insulin therapy the suspension may be used as basal insulin (evening and/or morning injection) with fast-acting insulin given at meals.
The individual insulin requirement is usually between 0.3 and 1.0 international unit/kg/day.

items.t: Biphasic 30/70: ready-made mixture so patients do not need to mix insulins; regimen based on individual metabolic needs, dose set by the physician.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia warning symptoms may be less pronounced or different with much improved control, long-standing diabetes, diabetic neuropathy, after a change of insulin, or with medicines such as beta-blockers. Uncorrected hypo- or hyperglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness, coma or death.

src.q: Other conditions which may make the early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia different or less pronounced include long duration of diabetes, diabetic nerve disease, or medications such as beta blockers.
Uncorrected hypoglycaemic and hyperglycaemic reactions can cause loss of consciousness, coma or death.

items.t: Inadequate doses or stopping treatment (especially insulin-dependent diabetes) can cause hyperglycaemia and potentially lethal diabetic ketoacidosis.

src.q: may lead to hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis; conditions which are potentially lethal
Inadequate dosing or discontinuation of treatment, especially in type 1 diabetes, may lead to hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis.

items.t: Insulin needs may change markedly with adrenal, pituitary or thyroid disease and with renal or hepatic impairment; they rise with illness (especially infection and fever) or emotional upset; change with exercise or diet.

src.q: Insulin requirements may change significantly in diseases of the adrenal, pituitary or thyroid glands and in the presence of renal or hepatic impairment.
Concomitant illness, especially infections and feverish conditions, usually increases the patient's insulin requirement.

items.t: Rotate injection sites (lipodystrophy, cutaneous amyloidosis); monitor blood glucose after a site change.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to perform continuous rotation of the injection site to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis.
A sudden change in the injection site to an unaffected area has been reported to result in hypoglycaemia.

items.t: With pioglitazone: watch for heart failure, weight gain and oedema; stop pioglitazone if cardiac symptoms worsen.

src.q: patients should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure, weight gain and oedema. Pioglitazone should be discontinued, if any deterioration in cardiac symptoms occurs.

items.t: Soluble insulin should not be used in pumps (one SmPC: risk of precipitation in pump catheters); suspensions are not for pumps.

src.q: Due to the risk of precipitation in pump catheters, Actrapid should not be used in insulin pumps for continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
Insulin suspensions are not to be used in insulin infusion pumps.

items.t: Check the insulin label before each injection. Seek advice before travel across time zones.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to always check the insulin label before each injection to avoid accidental mix-ups between Actrapid and other insulin products.

src.q: Insulin requirements may be reduced in the presence of substances with hypoglycaemic activity, such as oral hypoglycaemics (OHA), salicylates (for example, acetylsalicylic acid), certain antidepressants (monoamine oxidase inhibitors)

src.q: Insulin requirements may be increased by substances with hyperglycaemic activity, such as glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, growth hormone, danazol, beta2- sympatomimetics (such as ritodrine, salbutamol, terbutaline), thiazides.

items.t: Beta-blockers may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms. Octreotide/lanreotide may raise or lower requirement. Alcohol may intensify or reduce the effect.

src.q: Beta-blockers may mask the symptoms of hypoglycaemia.

items.t: GLP-1 receptor agonists (MHRA): when one is added to insulin, an insulin dose reduction may be considered to lower hypoglycaemia risk, but reduce insulin stepwise with blood glucose self-monitoring; abrupt reduction or stopping of insulin has led to diabetic ketoacidosis. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not substitutes for insulin.

src.q: blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary when adjusting the dose of insulin, particularly when GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy is initiated and insulin is reduced

items.t: No restriction on insulin in pregnancy (insulin does not cross the placenta); poorly controlled diabetes (hypo- or hyperglycaemia) raises the risk of malformation and death in utero. Keep good control and monitor glucose and general health closely; requirements usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and fall quickly after delivery.

items.t: Severe hypoglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness, convulsions or death. Mild: oral glucose or sugar. Moderately severe: glucagon IM/SC then oral carbohydrate. No response to glucagon (or not available): IV glucose. Give a meal on recovery; observe, as hypoglycaemia may recur.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia may lead to loss of consciousness, and in extreme cases, death.
Correction of moderately severe hypoglycaemia can be accomplished by intramuscular or subcutaneous administration of glucagon, followed by oral carbohydrate when the patient recovers sufficiently.
Patients who fail to respond to glucagon must be given glucose solution intravenously.

items.t: Systemic allergy is very rare but may be life-threatening (whole-body rash, breathlessness, wheeze, low blood pressure, fast pulse, sweating); treat immediately; a change of insulin or desensitisation may be needed.

src.q: Systemic allergy, which is very rare (< 1/10,000) but potentially more serious, is a generalised allergy to insulin.
